title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
authors: Yue Wu, Haoyu Wan, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

infographic.key_insight: Specialized, physics-aware machine learning force fields are needed to reliably simulate complex materials dynamics where general-purpose MLIPs break down under reactive, non-equilibrium, and large-scale fracture conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid mechanics and fracture simulations, task-specific ML force fields can extend atomistic accuracy to the length and time scales relevant to damage evolution, but only if they are validated against the target observables.
method: Assess MLIP design trade-offs: strained-state coverage, message-passing cost, and nonlocal interactions
Benchmark specialized potentials across four hard scenarios: electrified interfaces, open systems, multiphase evolution, and fracture
Use observable-specific validation rather than relying only on near-equilibrium zero-shot performance
infographic.evidence_signal: The review synthesizes evidence across four demanding application contexts to compare model behavior against intended observables, highlighting where pretrained equivariant GNNs succeed or fail.
infographic.watch_item: High-order architectures and extrapolation to highly strained or reactive states can be computationally expensive and unreliable without careful, application-specific training and validation.
infographic.paper_title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics

title: Deep learning driven framework for optimization of polycrystalline microstructures under competing strength requirements
authors: Ashwini Gupta, Indrashish Saha, Lori Graham-Brady, Tamer A. Zaki
abstract: Computational design of polycrystalline microstructures for enhanced mechanical performance requires repeated high-fidelity simulations over stochastic morphologies, rendering conventional crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) approaches prohibitively expensive for optimization. Here, we develop a deep learning-driven framework for optimizing polycrystalline microstructures under competing quasi-static and dynamic performance requirements. A 3D U-Net surrogate maps polycrystalline copper microstructures directly to full-field velocity histories from plate-impact simulations, preserving the spatial and temporal resolution needed to evaluate dynamic performance and interrogate underlying wave interactions and failure mechanisms. The surrogate is coupled with stochastic microstructure generation and derivative-free optimization to efficiently navigate the design space. To monitor surrogate reliability during optimization, we introduce a distribution-consistent reliability region (DCRR) based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to quantify distributional shift from the training data. The framework is demonstrated for multiple design problems, including constrained optimization of spall and yield strengths and inverse design. The optimal designs are validated using CPFE simulations with less than 3% prediction error across all optimization cases, while the surrogate-driven optimization reduces cumulative evaluation time by approximately four orders of magnitude compared with direct CPFE-based optimization. Although demonstrated here for the design of polycrystalline microstructures targeting spall and yield strengths, the framework is broadly applicable to optimization problems where high-fidelity full-field simulations are prohibitively expensive but spatially and temporally resolved response information is essential for evaluating, interpreting, and optimizing candidate designs.

infographic.key_insight: A deep learning surrogate combined with stochastic generation and optimization enables fast design of polycrystalline microstructures that balance competing spall and yield strength targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical route to microstructure optimization when repeated crystal plasticity simulations are too expensive for design studies.
method: 3D U-Net maps 3D polycrystalline copper morphologies to full-field velocity histories from plate-impact CPFE simulations.
Derivative-free optimization searches the microstructure space using surrogate predictions instead of repeated high-fidelity solves.
A distribution-consistent reliability region based on MMD tracks when optimization moves outside the training-data manifold.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated optimal designs matched CPFE with under 3% prediction error, and surrogate-driven optimization cut cumulative evaluation time by about four orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on staying within a reliable distributional region, so out-of-distribution microstructures may need additional training data or stricter trust-region control.
infographic.paper_title: Deep learning driven framework for optimization of polycrystalline microstructures under competing strength requirements

title: A Localized Hybrid Finite Element--Random Feature Method for Elliptic Interface Problems on Unfitted Meshes
authors: Siyuan Lang, Zhiyue Zhang
abstract: We develop a localized hybrid finite element--random feature method (FEM--RFM) for elliptic interface problems on unfitted background meshes. The central idea is to use the random feature method (RFM) only in the narrow band formed by interface-cut cells of a uniform Cartesian background mesh,while retaining standard $Q_p$ finite elements on the remaining uncut cells. Within the band, local RFM representations are used on the two physical sides of the interface. The prescribed jumps in the solution and normal flux are incorporated through residual equations involving the two RFM representations on the physical interface $Γ$, while the finite element method (FEM) and RFM components are coupled across a separate grid-aligned artificial interface $Γ_c$ through trace and variational normal-flux residuals. A Schur reduction eliminates the interior finite element unknowns through sparse solves while retaining their Galerkin equations as equality constraints. The remaining band and interface residuals are minimized in a reduced least-squares problem involving only the coupling nodal values and random-feature coefficients. The method is assessed numerically on a range of two- and three-dimensional interface problems involving high coefficient contrasts, nonsmooth and multiple interfaces, and irregular outer boundaries, together with an application-oriented thermal-homogenization problem for a periodic bicontinuous composite.

infographic.key_insight: A localized hybrid FEM–random feature approach can solve elliptic interface problems on unfitted meshes by using standard finite elements away from the interface and random features only in the narrow cut-cell band.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces the high cost of global surrogate representations while preserving accuracy for challenging multi-physics interface problems with coefficient jumps, irregular geometries, and high contrast.
method: Use standard Qp FEM on uncut background cells.
Use local random-feature representations only in interface-cut cells on both physical sides of the interface.
Enforce jump and flux conditions on the true interface, then couple FEM and RFM across an artificial grid-aligned interface via residual constraints and Schur reduction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is numerically evaluated in 2D and 3D on high-contrast, nonsmooth, multiple-interface, and irregular-boundary problems, including a thermal-homogenization application.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds implementation complexity because it requires accurate interface localization, residual coupling across two interfaces, and efficient sparse elimination for the interior FEM unknowns.
infographic.paper_title: A Localized Hybrid Finite Element--Random Feature Method for Elliptic Interface Problems on Unfitted Meshes

title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications
authors: Jairo Rondon, Juan Valera, Alex Velez Cruz, Irela Perez Magin
abstract: Ceramic materials are inorganic, predominantly nonmetallic solids whose performance is governed by the interplay among atomic bonding, crystal structure, processing, microstructure, and functional properties. Their ionic and covalent bonding provides high hardness, thermal and chemical stability, wear resistance, and diverse electrical behavior, but also limits plastic deformation and increases sensitivity to flaws, porosity, grain boundaries, and residual stresses. This review examines ceramics through the processing--microstructure--property--performance relationship, emphasizing the effects of crystal chemistry, defects, grain size, porosity, and phase stability on mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior. Conventional sintering, sol--gel processing, and additive manufacturing are discussed as key routes for controlling densification, porosity, geometry, and composition. Biomedical ceramics, including alumina, zirconia, calcium phosphates, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, and bioactive glasses, are also reviewed. Emerging topics include nanoceramics, smart ceramics, composites, multimaterial manufacturing, defect engineering, immunomodulatory bioceramics, and sustainable processing. Major challenges remain in brittle fracture, processing heterogeneity, degradation control, scale-up, and the porosity--strength trade-off. Future advances will require integrating advanced manufacturing, multiscale characterization, predictive modeling, and data-driven design.

infographic.key_insight: Ceramics are performance-engineered by controlling bonding, processing, and microstructure, but their brittleness and flaw sensitivity remain the central design constraint.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper connects processing routes and defect control to mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biomedical performance, making it directly relevant to ceramic design, manufacturing, and reliability engineering.
method: Reviews the processing–microstructure–property–performance relationship in ceramics
Compares conventional sintering, sol–gel processing, and additive manufacturing
Covers biomedical ceramics, nanoceramics, composites, and emerging defect-engineering strategies
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a review paper synthesizing reported relationships and trends rather than presenting new experimental data or a single evaluation dataset.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation concern is the persistent porosity–strength trade-off, especially when scaling up manufacturing or using heterogeneous additive processes.
infographic.paper_title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications

title: A volume-controlled level-set method for topology optimization
authors: Wei Gong, Zhenmin Zhang, Shengfeng Zhu
abstract: Topology optimization typically involves a geometric volume/mass constraint due to the limited use of material. As a popular technique for topology optimization, the level-set method typically employs the Lagrange method, the penalty method, or the augmented Lagrangian approach to address the volume constraint. This requires careful parameter tuning and may lead to non-monotonic changes in the objective. In this paper, we present a new volume-controlled level-set method for topology optimization. By imposing a scalar weighted volume?compatibility constraint in a modified Stokes-type extension-regularization problem, the velocity is made volume compatible at the beginning of each frozen transport interval. At the continuous level, we prove that the initial rate of change of the regularized volume vanishes and that the subsequent frozen-velocity drift is of order $T^2$; under a narrow-band assumption, the corresponding constant is independent of the smoothing parameter. For the discontinuous Galerkin spatial semi-discretization of the level-set transport equation, we derive a quantitative regularized-volume drift estimate that displays the dependence on the smoothing parameter, spatial mesh size, transport time, and discrete velocity. The effectiveness of the present algorithm is demonstrated through the minimum compliance problem for linear elasticity, the eigenfrequency maximization for structural vibration, and the minimum energy dissipation problem for Stokes flows.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a level-set topology optimization method that directly controls volume by enforcing a scalar weighted volume-compatibility condition, reducing the need for delicate constraint tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives structural and fluid designers a more stable way to satisfy material-usage limits while optimizing compliance, vibration, or dissipation performance.
method: Modify the Stokes-type extension-regularization step so the initial level-set velocity is volume compatible.
Use frozen transport intervals to keep volume drift small, with a continuous-time drift of order T^2.
Derive a discontinuous Galerkin semi-discrete error/drift estimate showing dependence on smoothing, mesh size, transport time, and discrete velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on three benchmark classes: minimum compliance in linear elasticity, eigenfrequency maximization, and minimum energy dissipation for Stokes flow.
infographic.watch_item: The method’s accuracy and volume control still depend on smoothing, mesh resolution, and frozen-interval settings, so implementation choices may affect robustness.
infographic.paper_title: A volume-controlled level-set method for topology optimization

title: Quantification of plastic deformation in anorthite using micropillar compression
authors: Sarah Incel, Chunhua Tian, Anja Schreiber, Vladimir Roddatis, Sandra Korte-Kerzel
abstract: Plagioclase is the most abundant mineral group of the crust and will therefore either control or strongly influence crustal rheology. Yet, we still know little about crystal plasticity in plagioclase as brittle deformation dominates under most laboratory conditions. To overcome past challenges in quantifying crystal plastic deformation in plagioclase, we used micropillar compression to quantify the strength of specific slip systems as well as the stresses necessary for mechanical twinning in anorthite. Pillars with diameters of around 1 micrometre were milled from three differently oriented cuts of the same anorthite single crystals using focused-ion beam. Uniaxial deformation of 36 pillars in total was then conducted inside a scanning-electron microscope under either 25, 300, or 800 degrees Celsius. Most pillars were deformed with a constant displacement rate that corresponds to a strain rate of around 0.001 1/s on the pillars. We find that the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for mechanical (pericline) twinning lies at around 300 MPa and is, as expected from previous studies on other materials, insensitive to changes in temperature or strain rate. Pillar deformation in crystals oriented to activate slip exhibit a strong decrease in yield stress with increasing temperature. Among the deformation mechanisms active during pillar deformation, twinning is the easiest under the applied conditions, followed by slip on (011)[100] regardless of temperature. Slip on (011)[0-11] or (0-11)[011] is consistently the hardest mechanism to activate in our anorthite pillars.

infographic.key_insight: Micropillar compression reveals that in anorthite, mechanical twinning is easier to activate than slip, and slip strength drops strongly with temperature while twinning CRSS stays near 300 MPa.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results help constrain crystal-plastic constitutive models for plagioclase-rich crustal rocks, improving predictions of deformation, anisotropy, and rheology under geologic conditions.
method: Focused-ion-beam milled ~1 µm micropillars from three crystal orientations of an anorthite single crystal.
Compressed 36 pillars inside an SEM at 25, 300, and 800 °C.
Used constant displacement-rate loading to infer CRSS and compare twinning vs. slip activation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports orientation-dependent pillar deformation data showing ~300 MPa CRSS for pericline twinning, temperature-insensitive twinning, and a strong temperature dependence of yield stress for slip-active pillars.
infographic.watch_item: Micropillar tests probe highly localized deformation in small volumes, so extrapolating directly to bulk crustal behavior should account for size effects and crystal-orientation sensitivity.
infographic.paper_title: Quantification of plastic deformation in anorthite using micropillar compression

title: Phase-Field Fracture Simulation of Highly Deformable Thin Structures via a Discrete Differential Geometry Framework
authors: Bohan Zhang, Bo Wang, Huajiang Ouyang, Zhigang Wu, Yu Zhou, Weicheng Huang
abstract: Thin elastic flexible structures exploit large geometric deformation to achieve mechanical functionality, making their fracture behavior strongly coupled with the evolving structural configuration. This work presents a unified discrete differential geometry (DDG) phase-field framework for fracture in highly deformable thin structures. Membrane and bending elasticity are formulated from discrete geometric measures on a triangulated midsurface, while the phase field is defined on the same discrete surface to describe onset of crack growth and subsequent propagation. The coupled problem is solved using a staggered scheme, with phase-field irreversibility enforced by an active-set method. A degradation-deletion procedure removes nearly fully failed elements and reconstructs the DDG topology, enabling complete crack opening and substantial post-fracture reconfiguration. For two-dimensional in-plane fracture problems, the DDG predictions agree closely with geometrically nonlinear finite element results in both crack evolution and mechanical response. In three-dimensional tearing, the framework resolves the interaction between out-of-plane deformation and crack propagation, including the experimentally observed convergence and coalescence of initially parallel cracks. Its engineering applicability is further demonstrated using an island--bridge structure representative of flexible electronics. The simulations capture direction-dependent deformation modes, instability and snap-through during loading, and the coupled evolution of structural configuration and fracture. These results establish the proposed framework as an effective tool for investigating geometry-dependent fracture and supporting the damage-tolerant design of flexible thin structures.

infographic.key_insight: A unified discrete differential geometry phase-field model can simulate fracture in highly deformable thin structures while capturing the strong coupling between large geometric deformation and crack evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps predict failure, snap-through, and post-fracture reconfiguration in flexible thin structures, supporting more damage-tolerant designs for applications such as flexible electronics.
method: Phase field is defined directly on a triangulated midsurface to model crack initiation and growth.
Membrane and bending energies are computed from discrete geometric measures in a DDG formulation.
A staggered solver with active-set irreversibility and degradation-deletion enables full crack opening and topology updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports close agreement with geometrically nonlinear finite element results for 2D fracture and captures experimentally observed crack convergence/coalescence in 3D tearing and island-bridge flexible-electronics examples.
infographic.watch_item: The degradation-deletion and topology reconstruction steps may be implementation-sensitive and could affect robustness or accuracy near highly complex crack patterns.
infographic.paper_title: Phase-Field Fracture Simulation of Highly Deformable Thin Structures via a Discrete Differential Geometry Framework

title: Numerical Neural Operator: Connection Between Numerical Analysis and the Operator Learning and Building Discretized Neural Operators from Finite Element Methods
authors: Zecheng Zhang
abstract: Operator learning aims to learn mappings between function spaces and has been widely used for PDE-related problems. This raises two fundamental questions. First, is there a connection between standard numerical methods and neural operators, given that both are designed to approximate PDE solution operators? Second, when a neural operator is trained on numerically generated data, does it approximate the underlying infinite dimension operator, the training data themselves, or the discretized numerical scheme used to generate them? A key hypothesis in the paper is that the trained neural operator may mimic the discretized numerical schemes that generate the training data. The hypothesis has been partially and preliminary verified by the linear approximation principle proposed in Chen Chen 1995 paper and the following scaling law papers. However, neural operator approximation from the perspective of numerical discretization remains unexplored. In this work, we consider a class of PDEs and derive neural operator architectures from the numerical schemes. Firstly, the numerical basis functions, such as finite element basis functions, can be approximated or directly constructed by learnable neural networks. Then the finite difference schemes for temporal discretization can be unrolled into iterative neural architectures that generate the coefficients of the basis of the resulting neural operator. By leveraging numerical analysis, we establish convergence error estimates for these numerically derived neural operators. Notably, the network size depends polynomial on the approximation error in $L_2$, improving the nested exponential dependence derived in the general neural operator approximation and aligning with the numerical observations. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate reduced errors and improved parameter efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that neural operators can be constructed from finite element and time-stepping schemes, suggesting they may learn the discretized numerical solver rather than the continuous PDE operator directly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a numerically grounded path to build more parameter-efficient surrogate models for PDE simulation in solid mechanics and related engineering applications.
method: Approximate or learn FEM basis functions with neural networks.
Unroll finite-difference time discretization into an iterative neural architecture.
Use numerical analysis to derive convergence/error bounds for the resulting operator.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments showing reduced errors and improved parameter efficiency, alongside theoretical convergence estimates with polynomial dependence on approximation error.
infographic.watch_item: Because the architecture is tied to a specific discretization, performance and interpretation may depend strongly on the chosen mesh, basis, and time-stepping scheme.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Neural Operator: Connection Between Numerical Analysis and the Operator Learning and Building Discretized Neural Operators from Finite Element Methods

title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates
authors: Raj Maurya, Joyprakash Akhuli, Doyel Pandey
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for multiphysics modeling, yet fluid flow in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates remains largely unexplored because the governing operators are singular at the axis and momentum and energy are strongly coupled through advection and buoyancy. We introduce SAGE-PINN, a Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for this class of problems. SAGE-PINN removes the coordinate singularity by construction: the parity-preserving variable $s=r^2$ and a modified stream-function representation eliminate explicit $1/r$ terms from the trained residuals and satisfy mass conservation identically. Boundary-fitted analytical ansätze enforce the boundary conditions exactly, while staged momentum-thermal-joint training, residual normalization, Péclet- and Richardson-number continuation, and a physics-scaled drift guard stabilize the coupled optimization. The framework is trained without labelled data, using only physics and boundary constraints, and its predictions are validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer through a stenosed artery over a wide range of flow and thermal regimes, without case-specific tuning. Mass conservation remains at single-precision round-off, and over the central operating range the axial velocity and temperature are reproduced within $1.6\%$ and $9.1\%$ relative $L_2$ error, respectively. The main deterioration occurs only in the limiting regimes of strongly buoyancy-influenced slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer. Embedding cylindrical geometry, conservation structure, and boundary physics directly into the network provides a robust route to PINN simulation of axisymmetric multiphysics flows.

infographic.key_insight: SAGE-PINN embeds axisymmetric cylindrical geometry, parity-preserving variables, and exact boundary ansätze into a PINN to remove the axis singularity and enforce mass conservation by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables mesh-free simulation of coupled flow and heat transfer in axisymmetric devices such as stenosed arteries, with no labeled training data and robust performance across varying buoyancy and advection regimes.
method: Use the transformed radial variable s = r^2 and a modified stream-function form to eliminate explicit 1/r singular terms.
Enforce boundary conditions exactly with analytical boundary-fitted ansätze and train in staged momentum-thermal-joint phases.
Stabilize optimization with residual normalization, Péclet-/Richardson-number continuation, and a physics-scaled drift guard.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer, the model kept mass conservation at single-precision round-off and achieved up to 1.6% axial-velocity and 9.1% temperature L2 error over the central operating range.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy degrades in the extreme regimes of strongly buoyancy-driven slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer, so continuation and scaling choices may need careful tuning there.
infographic.paper_title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates

title: An extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation
authors: Han Zhang, Mehrisadat Makki Alamdari, Babak Shahbodagh, Mohammad Vahab, Cosmin Anitescu, Timon Rabczuk
abstract: Thermo-mechanical fracture couples transient heat conduction on a cracked domain with a crack that grows as the temperature and the displacement evolve. Neural energy solvers have been proposed for phase-field fracture and later extended to represent a sharp crack through the network input, but heat conduction on the cracked domain and crack propagation under the resulting thermal stresses have not yet been treated together in these solvers. We present an extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation in which the crack remains a sharp polyline. Two networks represent the temperature and the displacement and receive the crack through a scalar embedding function, discontinuous across the crack and smooth elsewhere, so that both fields can jump across it without a regularization length, and the displacement is enriched near the tip by the Williams expansion with trainable amplitudes. The two fields are obtained by minimizing an incremental conduction functional and the thermoelastic potential energy in a staggered sequence, with Monte Carlo integration on points stratified over background elements, densified near the tip and redrawn during training. The stress intensity factors are extracted by the interaction integral with the area term of Wilson and Yu and checked by a sweep of the contour radius, and the crack advances at the maximum hoop stress angle when the energy release rate of the kink reaches the critical value at the crack-tip temperature. On a stationary thermal edge crack the extracted stress intensity factor agrees with the published value to 0.11%, in a functionally graded shear test initiation agrees with an independent sharp-crack finite element solution to within one load step, and on a notched cruciform specimen the crack paths follow the published solutions under mechanical, thermal and combined loading.

infographic.key_insight: A sharp-crack deep energy method is extended to jointly solve transient heat conduction and thermo-mechanical crack growth by encoding the crack directly into the neural inputs and advancing the crack with a fracture criterion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables physics-informed prediction of crack initiation and path evolution under thermal, mechanical, and combined loading without introducing a phase-field regularization length.
method: Two neural networks approximate temperature and displacement on a cracked domain using a discontinuous scalar crack embedding.
The displacement field is further enriched near the crack tip with a Williams expansion with trainable amplitudes.
Training alternates minimization of conduction and thermoelastic energy with Monte Carlo sampling, while crack advance uses interaction-integral SIFs and the maximum hoop-stress criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method matches a published thermal edge-crack stress intensity factor within 0.11% and reproduces benchmark crack initiation and paths on graded and cruciform specimens.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on careful crack-tip sampling, contour-radius checks for SIF extraction, and stable coupling between thermal and mechanical updates.
infographic.paper_title: An extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation

title: Dislocation mediated twin boundary faceting in $β$-Sn
authors: John Israel, Ian Chesser, Khanh Dang, Vinamra Agrawal
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs), including twin boundaries (TBs), play a critical role in plastic deformation by interacting with dislocations. The deformation and strengthening mechanisms in $β$-Sn are of significant interest because Sn-based alloys are widely used as solder materials. Recent experiments have shown deformation-induced faceting in $β$-Sn arising from twin-dislocation interactions. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations informed by a recently developed machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP), we demonstrate a $\langle c\rangle$ dislocation-absorption mediated faceting reaction along $(301)$ TBs in $β$-Sn in which facet length grows with the number of absorbed dislocations. We show that the predicted facet length is consistent with isotropic elasticity theory only when the disclination character of the asymmetric twin facet is taken into account. We discuss analogies to faceting reactions in other low symmetry metals and hypothesize that the ubiquity of $(301)$ twins in $β$-Sn stems from their ability to grow rapidly through a forest of dislocation obstacles.

infographic.key_insight: Molecular dynamics shows that in β-Sn, ⟨c⟩ dislocations can be absorbed by (301) twin boundaries and drive a faceting reaction whose facet length increases with each absorbed dislocation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mechanism helps explain how Sn-based solder microstructures may evolve under plastic loading, affecting twin-boundary stability, strength, and damage tolerance.
method: MD simulations of β-Sn twin-dislocation interactions
Machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) for atomistic accuracy
Elasticity-based interpretation including disclination effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors compare simulated facet-length growth against isotropic elasticity theory and report agreement only when the asymmetric twin facet’s disclination character is included.
infographic.watch_item: The faceting prediction depends on atomistic simulations and a specific MLIP, so transferability to other loads, temperatures, or alloy chemistries may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Dislocation mediated twin boundary faceting in $β$-Sn

title: Quantitative Eshelby stability: local and finite-shape theory through AI-assisted mechanics
authors: Bo Ni
abstract: How can human researchers use artificial intelligence (AI) to make progress on difficult mechanics problems while retaining control of physical significance, mathematical rigor, and validation? We explore this opportunity through a quantitative stability problem rooted in the Eshelby conjecture. For a uniform dilatational eigenstrain in a homogeneous isotropic solid, we establish a nonlinear two-sided relation between whole-interior strain heterogeneity and a geometry-only distance from the ellipsoid family, with half-order Sobolev scaling that captures morphological length scale. We then develop a complementary finite-shape theory: ellipsoidal subtraction yields an exact residual-field budget from which systematically convergent upper and lower bounds are obtained for a prescribed geometry. Applied to protruded, indented, and necked inclusions, the bounds agree with independent displacement-based finite-element calculations. The study also documents a human-led, AI-assisted research process in which researchers select consequential problems, shape targets, audit arguments, require independent checks, and interpret mechanics, while AI broadens analytical exploration and supports computation. This experience also led us to develop Open Problems in Mechanics, a versioned community-facing map that makes selected mechanics questions, their known/open boundaries, and criteria for progress explicit.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns the Eshelby stability question into a quantitative geometry-vs-strain framework, linking interior strain heterogeneity to distance from ellipsoidal shape with rigorous scaling laws.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides practical bounds for evaluating and designing non-ellipsoidal inclusions, helping predict mechanical stability and validate finite-element models in solid mechanics.
method: Derive a nonlinear two-sided relation between whole-interior strain heterogeneity and a geometry-only distance to the ellipsoid family.
Use half-order Sobolev scaling to capture morphological length-scale effects.
Develop ellipsoidal subtraction to obtain residual-field budgets and convergent upper/lower bounds for specific inclusion shapes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The proposed bounds were tested on protruded, indented, and necked inclusions and agreed with independent displacement-based finite-element calculations.
infographic.watch_item: The framework relies on careful shape characterization and rigorous interpretation, so its practical use may be sensitive to geometry measurement error and to cases outside the stated isotropic, uniform-dilatational setting.
infographic.paper_title: Quantitative Eshelby stability: local and finite-shape theory through AI-assisted mechanics

title: On the Convergence of the Mesh-Free Discretization of a Non-Linear Bond-Based Peridynamic Model with a Bond-Breakage Criterion
authors: Lukas Pflug, Michael Stingl, Max Zetzmann
abstract: We show the convergence of a commonly used mesh-free discretization of a dynamic non-linear bond-based peridynamic model with irreversible damage implemented via a bond-breakage criterion for a fixed horizon $δ>0$. The model chosen here is a mathematically well-posed regularization of a discontinuous peridynamic operator often found in the literature, which assumes that fracture results from strain in tension only. We explicitly include the one-point quadrature used in this scheme in the analysis. The convergence is with respect to the natural norm of the solution space given by $C^1([0,T],L^\infty(Ω)^d)$, and therefore $L^\infty(Ω)^d$ in the spatial coordinates. This result heavily constrains the spatial regularity of the continuous solution which we prove afterwards. More specifically, for locally $L$-Lipschitz continuous input data, local Lipschitz bounds are derived for the displacement, regardless of damage. This is consistent with interpreting the peridynamic model used here as an approximation to a truly discontinuous fracture model with a length-scale parameter given by the horizon $δ>0$. We note that we do not deal with the limit of the solutions as $δ\searrow 0$.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proves that a standard mesh-free discretization of a nonlinear bond-based peridynamic fracture model converges for a fixed horizon, even with irreversible bond breakage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives mathematical assurance that common peridynamic fracture simulations can be trusted at the discretization level before studying the more difficult zero-horizon limit.
method: Analyze a well-posed regularized dynamic peridynamic model with tension-driven bond breakage.
Include the practical one-point quadrature used in mesh-free schemes directly in the convergence proof.
Establish convergence in C^1([0,T], L^\infty(Ω)^d) and derive local Lipschitz bounds for the displacement.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a convergence proof based on the natural solution norm and derives spatial regularity bounds for locally L-Lipschitz input data.
infographic.watch_item: The result is for a fixed horizon δ > 0 only, so it does not address the physically important limit as δ approaches 0.
infographic.paper_title: On the Convergence of the Mesh-Free Discretization of a Non-Linear Bond-Based Peridynamic Model with a Bond-Breakage Criterion

title: Toward Reliable Patient-Specific Aortic Strain Mapping from 4D CTA: Validation, Spectral Structure, and Clinical Potential
authors: Tricia Lobo, Wensi Wu, Harold I. Litt, Nimesh D. Desai, Alison M. Pouch
abstract: Objective: To develop and validate a framework for spatially resolved ascending aortic strain estimation from 4D computed tomography angiography (CTA) and characterize reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales. Methods: We constructed patient-specific aortic strain maps using nnU-Net segmentation, optimized surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation. Finite element (FE)-derived synthetic 4D CT sequences provided controlled reference deformations for registration validation. Strain reliability was characterized across segmentation sources and Laplace-Beltrami (LB) spectral scales. Associations with diameter, aortic height index (AHI), and age were assessed. Results: Registration-derived median strain showed minimal bias relative to FE-reference strain for observer-derived (0.0013) and nnU-Net-derived meshes (0.0056). Median strain exhibited low bias and narrow 95% limits of agreement (LoA) across segmentation sources (interobserver: bias = -0.0045, LoA [-0.0490, 0.0399]; nnU-Net versus observer: bias = -0.0052, LoA [-0.0340, 0.0237]). Differences were greater for 95th-percentile strain, particularly in the interobserver comparison. LB spectral analysis showed preferential preservation of low-frequency strain organization, with k = 5 reconstructions reducing segmentation-related disagreement by 52-56%. The 95th-percentile areal strain was inversely associated with maximum ascending aortic diameter (r = -0.493, p = 0.005), AHI (r = -0.488, p = 0.005), and age (r = -0.479, p = 0.006). Three high-grade AR cases showed heterogeneous regional strain patterns. Conclusion: This framework reproducibly estimates ascending aortic strain from 4D CTA, characterizes its reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales, and demonstrates its potential for noninvasive assessment of patient-specific aortic mechanics.

infographic.key_insight: A validated 4D CTA pipeline can recover patient-specific ascending aortic strain maps with good agreement to finite-element reference deformations and stable median strain across segmentation sources.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables noninvasive, spatially resolved assessment of aortic mechanics that may support risk stratification and study of aneurysm or valvular disease progression.
method: nnU-Net segmentation, surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation
Finite element synthetic 4D CT used as a controlled reference for validation
Laplace-Beltrami spectral reconstruction used to test strain robustness across spatial scales
infographic.evidence_signal: Median strain showed minimal bias versus FE-reference strain and narrow limits of agreement across observer and nnU-Net segmentations, while 95th-percentile strain varied more and related inversely to diameter, AHI, and age.
infographic.watch_item: High-percentile strain metrics are more sensitive to segmentation differences, so implementation should treat localized extremes with caution and validate segmentation quality carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Reliable Patient-Specific Aortic Strain Mapping from 4D CTA: Validation, Spectral Structure, and Clinical Potential

title: AtomWorld-Mirror: Macro-Step World Modeling of Critical Evolution Backbones for Materials Dynamics
authors: Ziming Pan, Ruge Zhang, Haozhi Han, Junkai Zhou, Xingyuan Chen, Yifeng Chen
abstract: Atomistic simulation is a fundamental tool for studying long-term materials evolution, from diffusion and defect dynamics to interfacial reactions and fracture. Yet conventional simulators typically advance at microscopic resolution, spending substantial computation on low-impact local updates before reaching structurally consequential states, an evolutionary-resolution bottleneck that limits long-horizon simulation. We propose AtomWorld-Mirror, a time-aware macro-step world model for the critical evolution backbone of atomic systems. For Step-Wise atomistic simulation, AtomWorld-Mirror distills short micro-event segments into physically reachable transitions between key states, jointly predicting sparse structural edits and accumulated physical time through latent macro-step dynamics. Local reachability, inventory conservation, and continuous-time consistency constrain each transition. By amortizing local atomic physics into a reusable latent macro model and replacing explicit micro-event replay with macro-step inference, this formulation provides a path toward substantially faster prediction of long-term materials evolution while preserving structural validity and time semantics. Across five atomic systems, spanning Cu-rich RPV steel irradiation aging, Cu-Zr metallic glass, and Li$_3$N-based anti-perovskite solid electrolyte, macro-step inference delivers a speed up of $10^3$ to $10^4$ times over event-by-event simulation.

infographic.key_insight: AtomWorld-Mirror replaces event-by-event atomistic simulation with a time-aware macro-step world model that predicts physically reachable state changes and elapsed time for long-horizon materials evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could enable much faster simulation of diffusion, damage, and fracture-related processes while preserving structural validity, making long-time materials design and reliability studies more practical.
method: Distills short micro-event segments into latent macro-step transitions between key atomic states.
Jointly predicts sparse structural edits and accumulated physical time.
Uses reachability, inventory conservation, and continuous-time consistency constraints to enforce physical plausibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five atomic systems, including Cu-rich RPV steel irradiation aging, Cu-Zr metallic glass, and Li3N-based anti-perovskite solid electrolyte, the method reports 10^3 to 10^4× speedups over event-by-event simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Macro-step predictions may be sensitive to how well the latent model generalizes to unseen chemistries, defect pathways, or loading conditions beyond the training regimes.
infographic.paper_title: AtomWorld-Mirror: Macro-Step World Modeling of Critical Evolution Backbones for Materials Dynamics

title: Energy conserving compatible space--time FEM for deterministic and stochastic rotating shallow water
authors: Maneesh Kumar Singh, Colin J. Cotter
abstract: We present a fully discrete energy conserving discretisation of the rotating shallow water equations with arbitrary order in space and time. A space time finite element discretisation is used, built from compatible finite element methods in space and continuous Petrov-Galerkin schemes in time. Projected auxiliary variables for Hamiltonian derivatives are necessary for exact energy conservation. We provide an iterative solver approach based on monolithic patch smoothers, which allows us to efficiently converge a Newton method sufficiently that energy errors due to the solver are very small. We extend this construction to the energy conserving Stochastic Forcing by Lie Transport formulation. Then we demonstrate the convergence, conservation and robustness in numerical tests.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete space-time compatible FEM can conserve energy exactly for rotating shallow water dynamics, including a stochastic forcing extension, by using projected auxiliary variables and compatible time discretization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a high-fidelity, structure-preserving solver blueprint for geophysical flow simulations where long-time stability, conservation, and robustness matter.
method: Compatible finite elements in space combined with continuous Petrov-Galerkin schemes in time
Projected auxiliary variables enforce exact Hamiltonian energy conservation
Monolithic patch smoothers accelerate Newton solves for the space-time system
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical tests demonstrating convergence, conservation, and robustness, with solver-induced energy errors kept very small.
infographic.watch_item: Exact conservation depends on sufficiently accurate nonlinear solves, so incomplete Newton convergence may reintroduce small energy errors.
infographic.paper_title: Energy conserving compatible space--time FEM for deterministic and stochastic rotating shallow water

title: Early-time dynamics of the Richtmyer-Meshkov instability at Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic interfaces
authors: Xuning Zhao, Mauro Rodriguez
abstract: The Richtmyer-Meshkov instability (RMI) is initiated when a shock wave interacts with a perturbed interface between two materials, imparting an initial velocity to the interfacial perturbation. When the materials are viscoelastic, the subsequent evolution is influenced by the coupled effects of inertia, viscous dissipation, and elastic resistance. The interplay of these effects remains poorly understood and is important for predicting the dynamic response of shock-loaded soft materials, e.g., in blast-induced injury. Using the incompressible Cauchy momentum equation with a Kelvin-Voigt constitutive model, we conduct a linear stability analysis for the early-time post-shock evolution of a single-mode interface perturbation of two viscoelastic materials. We derive an implicit dispersion relation for the temporal growth rates of the perturbation. This relation depends on density, viscosity, and elasticity contrasts between the two materials and an viscoelastic parameter which is a bounded ratio of the viscous dissipation and elastic resistance response rates. Four material cases, spanning symmetric to highly contrasted interfaces, are examined to show how the viscoelastic number affects the growth rate structure as complex-dominated (oscillatory) or real-dominated (monotonic relaxation). The critical viscoelastic number separates these two regimes and is primarily governed by the density and viscosity contrasts. These results provide a theoretical criterion for predicting the early-time response of shock-driven interfaces involving fluids and viscoelastic solids.

infographic.key_insight: A Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic interface can respond to shock-driven Richtmyer-Meshkov perturbations in either oscillatory or monotonic early-time modes, with a critical viscoelastic number separating the two behaviors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a theoretical criterion for predicting how shock-loaded soft materials, fluids, and viscoelastic solids will evolve immediately after impact, which is useful for blast and injury mechanics.
method: Linear stability analysis of the incompressible Cauchy momentum equation
Kelvin-Voigt constitutive model for two viscoelastic materials
Implicit dispersion relation derived for single-mode perturbation growth rates
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparison across four material cases spanning symmetric to highly contrasted interfaces to show how viscoelastic number, density contrast, and viscosity contrast change the growth-rate structure.
infographic.watch_item: The result is a linear, early-time theory for single-mode perturbations, so nonlinear effects and later-time interface evolution are not captured.
infographic.paper_title: Early-time dynamics of the Richtmyer-Meshkov instability at Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic interfaces

title: Rare Gate Disagreements Can Limit Plasticity: When Gradient Flow Mispredicts Finite-Batch SGD
authors: Ruoyu Zhao, Mingxuan Zhang, Jianbo Dai, Jiaqi Wu, Chenyu Zhu, Tong Che
abstract: Population gradient flow is a common tool for reasoning about how neural networks adapt, including after pretraining. We show that it can mispredict finite-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) qualitatively, and we trace the discrepancy to a specific mechanism. In a two-unit ReLU regression, a source task drives the two neurons toward positive proportionality and a target task rewards separating them. After source training for time $T$, gradient flow recovers on the target in time linear in $T$. Online SGD with batch size $b$ and step size $η$ in both phases instead fails with high probability throughout a horizon of order $e^{c/η}$ once $T \gtrsim \log(b/η)$, uniformly on an explicit set of initializations with Gaussian probability above one percent. For each fixed $T$, small-step SGD still recovers, so the failure requires the joint limit of small steps and long pretraining. At the target clone, the population instability is carried entirely by inputs on which the two ReLU gates disagree. For units at angle $δ$ these inputs form a wedge of probability $δ/π$, and weight decay shrinks the angle exponentially during pretraining. On every other input both units receive the same random linear update, which contracts their separation in conditional expectation. Bounding the cumulative probability of sampling the wedge along the exact online recursion, without a diffusion approximation, shows that recovery with fixed probability from an identical source-gradient-flow checkpoint, within $e^{c/η}$ updates, requires $Nb \gtrsim e^{λT}$ target samples and batch size $b \gtrsim ηe^{λT}$, where $N$ counts updates and $λ$ is the weight decay. In simulations, recovery is approximately a function of the disagreement budget $bδ/η$ and saturates in the horizon.

infographic.key_insight: Rare ReLU gate disagreements, not the average gradient, determine whether finite-batch SGD can recover after pretraining, so population gradient flow can be qualitatively wrong.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For staged training or fine-tuning, this means recovery may fail unless batch size and update budget are large enough to sample the small set of disagreeing inputs.
method: Two-unit ReLU regression with a source task that aligns neurons and a target task that separates them.
Compare population gradient flow with online SGD under batch size b and step size η after source pretraining time T.
Track the rare wedge of inputs where gates disagree and bound its cumulative sampling probability along the exact recursion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that, for T above about log(b/η), SGD can fail with high probability over a horizon of order e^{c/η}, while recovery from a gradient-flow checkpoint needs Nb ≳ e^{λT} and b ≳ ηe^{λT}; simulations show behavior collapses mainly as a function of bδ/η.
infographic.watch_item: The result is derived for a specific two-unit ReLU setup, so the threshold laws may not transfer directly to deeper or more realistic architectures without re-checking gate-disagreement dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Rare Gate Disagreements Can Limit Plasticity: When Gradient Flow Mispredicts Finite-Batch SGD

title: Stability-Plasticity Balance via Singular-Vector Selection in LLM Continual Learning
authors: Lingxiang Wang, Hainan Zhang, Liang Pang, Hongwei Zheng, Zhiming Zheng
abstract: Domain-specific continual adaptation of LLMs risks catastrophic forgetting, creating a fundamental tension between acquiring new capabilities and preserving those learned during pretraining. PEFT mitigates this problem by restricting the number of trainable parameters, but existing methods lack a principled unit for deciding where plasticity should be allocated and stability should be preserved. We identify the singular-vector channel as a natural unit for managing this trade-off. Each channel represents an input-output transformation, which can be updated to acquire new knowledge or fixed to preserve pretrained capabilities. Based on this perspective, we introduce SVC, a parameter-efficient continual-learning method that selectively updates Singular-Vector Channels. Before fine-tuning, SVC uses domain-specific data to estimate each channel's adaptation benefit and a fixed public general-domain corpus only as a history activation proxy for estimating forgetting cost. It then adaptively selects trainable channels based on these scores via knee-based cost screening, Pareto-front filtering, and Otsu thresholding. Experimental results across four LLM families and eight downstream tasks show that SVC better preserves pretrained capabilities while achieving strong downstream performance relative to existing PEFT baselines. Further analysis of channel scoring and selection demonstrates that selective plasticity at the singular-vector-channel level enables effective continual LLM adaptation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that continual LLM adaptation works best when plasticity is allocated at the singular-vector channel level, allowing the model to learn new domains while preserving pretrained knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a principled parameter-efficient strategy for managing the stability–plasticity trade-off in domain-specific model updating, which is critical for reliable deployment of large models in evolving engineering workflows.
method: Treat each singular-vector channel as a unit that can be either updated or frozen.
Estimate adaptation benefit from domain-specific data and forgetting cost from a fixed public general-domain corpus.
Select trainable channels using knee-based cost screening, Pareto-front filtering, and Otsu thresholding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments across four LLM families and eight downstream tasks indicate that SVC preserves pretrained capabilities better than PEFT baselines while maintaining strong downstream performance.
infographic.watch_item: The channel-selection pipeline depends on careful scoring and thresholding, so performance may be sensitive to corpus choice, task domain shift, and implementation details.
infographic.paper_title: Stability-Plasticity Balance via Singular-Vector Selection in LLM Continual Learning

title: Static Gradient Attribution Underperforms a Density-Matched Random Mask on Loss-Based Forgetting Within LoRA B-Matrix
authors: Yu Sun, Junwei Zhou, Zuodong Xiang, Yike Zhang, Pengcheng Xu, Xinyu Guan
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning updates a restricted subset of adapter parameters to incorporate sequential tasks while limiting catastrophic forgetting. Gradient attribution is a common rule for selecting that subset, but it requires an additional backward pass over calibration data. We identify a parameter-pool confound in comparisons between initialization-time gradient masks and unrestricted random masks under standard zero-initialized LoRA ($B=0$): the gradient with respect to $A$ is identically zero ($\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A=0$), so gradient masks select strictly from the $B$ matrix whereas unrestricted random masks draw from both $A$ and $B$. Such a comparison changes both the selection rule and the candidate parameter pool. Isolating the selection criterion by restricting both approaches to the same parameter pool, we find a negative result: a uniform random mask consistently achieves lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B. The effect is concentrated on the medical task, which contributes 80\% of the aggregate; code and math move in the same direction, and legal shows no reliable difference. This advantage is consistent with a stability--plasticity trade-off under the tested task sequence, in which random masking slightly reduces single-task fitting. On the two discrete-option tasks (Medical and Legal), the mean accuracy-BWT difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

infographic.key_insight: When LoRA starts with B=0, gradient attribution only searches the B matrix, so a same-pool random mask is a fairer comparison—and it surprisingly yields lower loss-based forgetting than gradient masking.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For parameter-efficient continual learning in constitutive modeling and other scientific fine-tuning settings, simpler random parameter selection may preserve prior-task performance better than gradient-based attribution under the tested setup.
method: Compare initialization-time gradient masking vs. uniform random masking
Control for the LoRA pool confound by restricting both methods to the same parameters
Measure backward transfer / forgetting across sequential tasks
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B, the same-pool random mask consistently beat gradient attribution on loss-based backward transfer, with the effect driven mostly by the medical task (80% of the aggregate).
infographic.watch_item: The result is specific to the tested task order, LoRA B=0 initialization, and model/dataset mix, so it should not be generalized without replication under different adapters and sequences.
infographic.paper_title: Static Gradient Attribution Underperforms a Density-Matched Random Mask on Loss-Based Forgetting Within LoRA B-Matrix
